About this document

This document provides the teaching content for Media, Journalism, and
Communications Years 12–13 of the New Zealand Curriculum.
Progress and assessment information for Media, Journalism, and Communications
Years 12–13 is still in development. Once that is completed, Media, Journalism, and
Communications Years 12–13 is proposed to be made by the Minister of Education as
a National Curriculum Statement under section 90(1)(a) of the Education and Training
Act 2020.
It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Media, Journalism, and Communications Years 12–13 will be required to
start using it in Year 12 from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January 2030.
This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

Students are taught how media messages are constructed, interpreted, and
distributed across a range of texts, products, forms and platforms, and how these
processes shape culture, communication, and public understanding. They examine
how meaning is created through media language, forms, representations, audiences,
institutions, and technologies, and how media can influence perceptions, values, and
behaviours.
Media, Journalism, and Communications provides students with the knowledge and
practices to critically analyse texts and products, evaluate information and
perspectives, investigate public issues, cultural narratives, and social change through
engagement with diverse local and global media, journalism, and communications
contexts. Students also create and communicate media content for a range of
purposes, audiences, and contexts, applying industry-informed conventions,
processes, and professional workflows to create, refine, and evaluate media
products.
As students progress through Year 12–13, they are taught to move beyond analysing
individual media texts to examining the wider social, cultural, technological, ethical,
and commercial forces that shape contemporary media environments. They develop
increasingly sophisticated capabilities to synthesise information and perspectives,
critique media systems, digital platforms, and emerging technologies, and evaluate
how these influence representation, participation, and the circulation of information.

Subject structure

Media, journalism, and communications are interconnected disciplines concerned with the creation, mediation, distribution, and interpretation of information, stories, and messages
across texts, products, platforms, and contexts. While the study of Media is one of the disciplines within this subject, the term media is also used in its broader sense throughout this
document to refer to the systems, technologies, texts, products, and practices through which information, stories, and messages are communicated within and across the three
disciplines.

 Disciplinary Writing

 Focus: the use of writing to reflect the ways in which knowledge is organised, analysed, and communicated within the discipline.
 In Media, Journalism, and Communications students use explicitly taught disciplinary writing to create and analyse media texts and products by understanding, applying, and
 evaluating language, codes, conventions, and structures for specific purposes and audiences.

Media, Journalism, and Communications | Years 12–13 | October 2026                                                                                                            Page 7

Products can include written (e.g. news articles, opinion pieces, reviews, scripts),
visual (e.g. films, trailers, music videos, posters), and aural (e.g. podcasts,
soundscapes) forms. By providing opportunities to experiment with and create
products throughout each year, students will strengthen their theoretical
understanding and practical skills in Media, Journalism and Communications.
Knowledge within the Production and Processes strand is intended to be integrated
throughout the teaching programme alongside the other strands in the curriculum.
The following tables outline production requirements in Years 12 and 13.

Media texts, products, and contexts

Media, Journalism, and Communications is an interdisciplinary subject that draws on
knowledge and practices from media, journalism, and communications. Students
should engage with a range of texts and products from across these disciplines to
explore how meanings are created, communicated, interpreted, and responded to in
different contexts.
Text and product selection should support opportunities for students to analyse,
interpret, compare, evaluate, and create media, journalism, and communications texts
and products for different purposes and audiences. Programmes should include a
diverse range of local and global texts and products, including Māori and Pacific
content in New Zealand media, and provide opportunities for students to engage with
a variety of perspectives, experiences, and voices.
Texts and products should be selected at an appropriate level of complexity for the
year level and provide opportunities for meaningful engagement through sustained
analysis, interpretation, evaluation, and production. Teachers may draw connections
across media, journalism, and communications contexts to support students to
understand both the distinctive features of each discipline and the ways they
intersect. Programmes should incorporate texts and products drawn from a range of
forms, including micro, short, long, and extended forms, to support breadth of learning
and engagement across media, journalism, and communications.
The following tables outline text form and range requirements in Years 12 and 13.
The Media, Journalism and Communications Curriculum Support Document provides
further guidance around appropriate media text selection.
